nameStory: The 'foxglove' part of this plant's name comes from its trumpet-shaped white flowers that look remarkably similar to the classic garden foxglove, though they're not closely related. The 'beardtongue' refers to a fuzzy, tongue-like structure (called a staminode) that sticks out from the flower's throat like a tiny beard. Touch the inside of a flower gently and you'll feel this soft, hairy projection that gives all Penstemon species their quirky common name.
description: Foxglove beardtongue is a sturdy perennial wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall with clusters of white, trumpet-shaped blooms. The plant forms neat clumps with smooth, lance-shaped leaves that clasp the sturdy stems. In summer, it sends up tall spikes packed with dozens of tubular flowers that look like tiny white foxgloves. It's the most common beardtongue east of the Mississippi River and has naturalized widely beyond its original Mississippi River basin home.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White, tubular flowers about 1 inch long cluster densely on tall spikes. Each flower has five petals fused into a trumpet shape with a fuzzy 'tongue' (staminode) visible inside the throat. The flowers feel slightly waxy and have a subtle sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, lance-shaped leaves with a waxy feel and slightly glossy surface. Lower leaves are broader and may have tiny teeth, while upper leaves clasp the stem directly without stalks. Run your finger along the edge - it feels smooth to slightly rough.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 2-4 feet tall with sturdy, four-angled stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers. Multiple flowering spikes emerge from each plant in a candelabra-like arrangement.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops small, egg-shaped capsules that split open to release tiny brown seeds. The dried capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken and persist into fall.

habitat: Look for foxglove beardtongue in sunny to partially shaded areas with well-drained soil, including meadows, prairie edges, roadsides, and open woodlands. It thrives in disturbed areas and has adapted well to New England's varied conditions, often appearing in old fields, along trails, and in naturalized garden settings. The plant tolerates both sandy and clay soils as long as drainage is decent.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as rosettes of glossy green leaves close to the ground. The distinctive waxy leaf texture becomes apparent as leaves expand in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak bloom time from June through August, with tall spikes of white flowers attracting bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. This is the best time for identification when flowers and fuzzy staminodes are clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, turning brown and splitting open. Basal leaves may remain green while upper stems begin to dry and turn brown.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and seed heads persist, creating architectural interest in the landscape. Basal rosettes of leaves may remain somewhat green under snow in protected areas.

funFact: Despite being called 'foxglove beardtongue,' this plant is actually more closely related to snapdragons than to true foxgloves - the similar flower shape is a case of convergent evolution, where unrelated plants develop similar features to attract the same pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with true foxglove (Digitalis), but foxglove beardtongue has white flowers and smooth leaves, while garden foxglove typically has purple, pink, or white flowers with fuzzy, wrinkled leaves. Memory trick: beardtongue leaves are smooth like a baby's skin, while true foxglove leaves feel rough and hairy like a beard.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'foxglove beardtongue,' this plant belongs to the plantain family (Plantaginaceae), not the foxglove family. The name similarity is purely based on flower shape. It's actually an introduced species in New England, having spread eastward from its native Mississippi River basin range, but it's now so well-established that many consider it naturalized.
compareHints: Among New England's beardtongues, foxglove beardtongue is the tallest and has the whitest flowers - hairy beardtongue has purple-pink flowers and fuzzy leaves, while pale beardtongue is much shorter with smaller, paler flowers. Foxglove beardtongue's smooth, waxy leaves and robust 3-4 foot height make it the most distinctive of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's beardtongues, hairy beardtongue is distinguished by its noticeably fuzzy stems and smaller purple flowers.
Among New England's beardtongues, pale beardtongue stands out for its very light, almost ghostly flower color compared to the bright white foxglove beardtongue or the purple-pink hairy beardtongue.
Long-sepal beardtongue stands out from other New England beardtongues primarily by its dramatically longer sepals and typically more colorful flowers.

Eastern gray beardtongue stands out from other New England beardtongues by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves - foxglove beardtongue has smooth green leaves, while hairy beardtongue is much shorter and has purple flowers.
